title: Contact Structures On 3-Manifolds
notes: Open the chapter as a navigation problem through a long source span. The central question is not only whether contact structures exist, but how to move between local models, global plane-field data, surface diagnostics, and classification results. The dependency-map miniature should signal that later theorems will be easier to remember if students can name which tool supplies construction, which supplies surface control, and which supplies rigidity.

title: The Learning Arc
notes: Frame the lecture in three passes. First come construction moves: Martinet, plane-field control, Lutz twists, and open books. Second come surface tools: characteristic foliations, elimination, convexity, and dividing sets. Third come consequences: Bennequin rigidity, overtwisted classification, tomography, and the tight classification anchors. Emphasize that the graph has fifteen nodes and eleven edges because it is a reading map, not a chronological proof list.

title: Martinet Construction
notes: Describe Martinet's construction as a global assembly theorem. A contact form on a solid torus is controlled by the curve r maps to h one of r and h two of r, while boundary data is tuned so that pieces can be glued. The point of this slide is the design pattern: a local contact inequality is converted into a boundary-matching tool for a closed three-manifold.

title: Plane-Field Homotopy Control
notes: The chapter does not treat contact structures as isolated forms. A cooriented plane field gives a Gauss map into the two-sphere, and regular values have preimage links carrying obstruction data. The Euler-class relation gives the first comparison between plane fields. The later Lutz move is powerful because it can alter contact geometry while keeping deliberate control over these homotopy coordinates.

title: Lutz Twist Path
notes: Use the h one h two plane as the easiest way to see the Lutz twist condition. The contact condition asks the radius derivative of the curve to rotate with positive oriented area, expressed by h one h two prime minus h one prime h two positive. Students should read the path as a contact torus model rather than as an arbitrary parametric curve.

title: Full Lutz Twist
notes: A full Lutz twist inserts a complete turn along a transverse knot. Its remarkable feature is that the homotopy class of the plane field can be left unchanged while the contact structure becomes overtwisted. The disk in the drawing is a witness, not a decoration: it marks the local feature that separates the flexible side of the classification story from the tight side.

title: Open Books As Alternate Existence
notes: Present open books as a second language for existence. A binding is surrounded by pages, and a contact structure is supported when alpha is positive on the binding and d alpha is positive on each page. The details are not the main proof load here; the lesson is that three-dimensional contact topology repeatedly translates between a global decomposition and local contact forms.

title: Tight Versus Overtwisted
notes: Separate the two worlds before introducing the surface technology. Overtwisted means that a particular disk appears, and once it appears, flexible classification takes over. Tight means no such disk is present, which makes the theory rigid enough to support inequalities and uniqueness theorems. This is the chapter's main fork: the same local contact condition has two very different global behaviors.

title: Characteristic Foliation Microscope
notes: Now zoom to a surface. For the graph z equals f of x and y in the standard contact form, restricting alpha gives a one-form on the surface. The characteristic direction is a vector annihilated by that restricted form. The local check records x dx plus y plus x dy for the radial graph and a zero residual at the origin, so the singular point is not a plotting accident.

title: Singularity Lab
notes: Use the three cases as a lightweight laboratory for how singularities move. The radial graph has equations x equals zero and y plus x equals zero. Tilting changes the first equation by one fifth, moving the singularity. The saddle reverses the y contribution, changing the linearized pattern. The point is to read characteristic foliations through equations, not through visual impression alone.

title: Elimination Lemma
notes: The elimination lemma is a surface-cleaning move. When an elliptic and hyperbolic singularity of the same sign are connected in the appropriate way, the characteristic foliation can be modified to remove the pair. Stress the local nature of the statement: the surrounding foliation is preserved outside a small neighborhood, so the move supports induction and simplification arguments on surfaces.

title: Genus And Euler Bound
notes: Before stating Bennequin, make the right side computable. The Euler characteristic of a Seifert surface converts topology into a numerical ceiling. For a disk the bound is minus one, for an annulus it is zero, and for a once-punctured torus it is one. The table also helps students see why the inequality is strongest for simple spanning surfaces.

title: Bennequin Inequality
notes: Treat the standard Legendrian unknot as a calibration point. Its Thurston-Bennequin contribution plus the absolute rotation is minus one; for a disk chi(D^2)=1, so minus chi(D^2)=-1. Equality is allowed in the tight standard model. The value of the slide is not the arithmetic alone; it shows how tightness can turn a surface into a hard numerical obstruction.

title: Convex Surface And Dividing Set
notes: Move from the full characteristic foliation to a compressed invariant. A convex surface has a transverse contact vector field, and the dividing set is where the associated function u vanishes. On the sphere picture, the equator is gamma, while the complement splits into positive and negative regions. The displayed alpha two of Y equals two z gives a concrete sign-changing model.

title: Giroux Flexibility
notes: Giroux flexibility explains why the dividing set is such efficient data. Once the dividing set is fixed and the compatibility conditions are met, different characteristic foliations can be realized by isotoping the surface in the contact manifold. The two panels deliberately keep the same equator while changing the leaf pattern, so the invariant is the dividing set rather than every individual leaf.

title: Overtwisted Classification
notes: This is the main flexible classification anchor. Fix an overtwisted disk Delta and compare the space of overtwisted contact structures with the space of plane fields. The inclusion is a weak homotopy equivalence, so plane-field homotopy data controls contact isotopy after the overtwisted witness is present. Contrast this with tight classification, where the same plane-field information is not enough.

title: Tomography
notes: Tomography is the tight-side habit of studying a three-manifold by slicing it with convex surfaces. In a product S two times an interval, one watches how dividing sets and boundary foliations evolve across the slices. The strong message is that tight structures can be forced by boundary data and controlled transitions, which is very different from overtwisted flexibility.

title: Tight Classification And Prime Decomposition
notes: Close by placing the named tight classification anchors in one dependency picture. The uniqueness results for S three, R three, S two times S one, and the three-ball relative to boundary foliation are fed by convex surface and tomography arguments. Prime decomposition then explains how connected sums inherit classification behavior. End by asking students to identify whether a future theorem is using construction, compression, or rigidity.
